fetched_contents.text: Rejection Mechanism of Ionic Solute Removal by Nanofiltration Membranes: An Overview Abstract The toxicity of heavy metals can cause water pollution and has harmful effects on human health and the environment. Various methods are used to overcome this pressing issue and each method has its own advantages and disadvantages. Membrane filtration technology such as nanofiltration (NF) produces high quality water and has a very small footprint, which results in lower energy usage. Nanofiltration is a membrane-based separation technique based on the reverse osmosis separation process developed in the 1980s. NF membranes have a pore size of 1 nm and molecular weight cut off (MWCO) of 300 to 500 Da. The properties of NF membranes are unique since the surface charge of the membranes is dependent on the functional groups of the membrane. The rejection mechanism of NF membrane is unique as it is a combination of various rejection mechanisms such as steric hindrance, electric exclusion, dielectric effect, and hydration mechanism. However, these mechanisms have not been studied in-depth due to their complexity. There are also many factors contributing to the rejection of NF membrane. Many junior researchers would face difficulty in studying NF membrane. Therefore, this paper is designed for researchers new to the field, and will briefly review the rejection mechanisms of NF membrane by both sieving and non-sieving separation processes. This mini-review aims to provide new researchers with a general understanding of the concept of the separation process of charged membranes. Keywords: nanofiltration, size exclusion, Donnan exclusion, membrane separation 1. Introduction Water pollution by heavy metals is known to be toxic and harmful to human health and the environment. As the human population grows, water pollution cannot be avoided due to humankind’s activities in various sectors, including industry, agriculture, and service. To evade this problem, several treatment technologies have been investigated by Crittenden et al. [1], such as reverse osmosis, disinfection, granular filtration, gravity separation, coagulation–flocculation, air stripping and aeration ion exchange, adsorption, and membrane filtration. Of these conventional treatments, membrane filtration technology has gained widespread popularity because of its numerous benefits in water treatment and its ability to achieve the required standard. Its benefits include space efficiency, remarkable energy reduction, and cost effectiveness [2]. In comparison, other conservative treatments are well-known for their ineffectiveness as well as production of hazardous products such as trichloromethane [3]. Furthermore, membrane filtration technology has the potential to close the gap between the economic and sustainability, environmental friendliness due to its less or no chemical requirement, and widespread accessibility [4]. As depicted in Figure 1, the membrane separation process is divided into three groups: the electrical-driven membrane process (electrodialysis and electrophoresis), the concentration-driven membrane process (pervaporation, membrane extraction), and the pressure-driven membrane process (microfiltration, ultrafiltration, nanofiltration, and reverse osmosis). Generally, in the membrane separation process, some substances are able to pass through (permeate) but some will be retained (retentate phase). According to Malliga et al. [5], the membrane filtration process (pressure-driven) is a method that uses membrane micropores to filter and employs selective permeability of membranes to separate particular substances in wastewater. A schematic representation of membrane filtration is displayed in Figure 2. As illustrated in Figure 2, the membrane acts as a barrier separating feed and permeate. The barriers considered here do not prevent the passage of all species but are permeable to some and impermeable to others. Since the number of species transported across a membrane is inversely related to its thickness, having the thinnest membrane feasible is favorable. Furthermore, pore aspect ratio and pore size distribution of the membrane also play an important role. It was found that increasing the pore aspect ratio improves membrane performance, while increasing the width of the pore size distribution deteriorates the performance [6]. Membrane performance is also dependent on process operating parameters such as feed concentration [7], feed flow rate, feed temperature, permeate vapor pressure [8] and applied pressure [9]. Each of these separation processes is distinctive since each of them works differently. The most critical factors in determining which separation process to use are efficiency and cost effectiveness [10]. Pirsaheb and colleagues took these two properties into account when comparing electrodialysis (ED) and reverse osmosis (RO) in order remove nitrate from drinking water. The results of their study showed that reverse osmosis is more efficient than electrodialysis in terms of cost per cubic meter of treated water and removal of nitrate and other chemical parameters. Therefore, their study distinguished that ED produces more waste energy than RO. The latest research [11] agreed with this conclusion; this research claimed that, in terms of capital cost, ED is less efficient than RO. It also asserts that estimates provided by industry showed that the area of normalized cost of ED is more than 200 $ m−2, while that of RO is less than 10 $ m−2. fetched_contents.text: Recent Advances in Membranes Used for Nanofiltration to Remove Heavy Metals from Wastewater: A Review Abstract The presence of heavy metal ions in polluted wastewater represents a serious threat to human health, making proper disposal extremely important. The utilization of nanofiltration (NF) membranes has emerged as one of the most effective methods of heavy metal ion removal from wastewater due to their efficient operation, adaptable design, and affordability. NF membranes created from advanced materials are becoming increasingly popular due to their ability to depollute wastewater in a variety of circumstances. Tailoring the NF membrane’s properties to efficiently remove heavy metal ions from wastewater, interfacial polymerization, and grafting techniques, along with the addition of nano-fillers, have proven to be the most effective modification methods. This paper presents a review of the modification processes and NF membrane performances for the removal of heavy metals from wastewater, as well as the application of these membranes for heavy metal ion wastewater treatment. Very high treatment efficiencies, such as 99.90%, have been achieved using membranes composed of polyvinyl amine (PVAM) and glutaraldehyde (GA) for Cr3+ removal from wastewater. However, nanofiltration membranes have certain drawbacks, such as fouling of the NF membrane. Repeated cleaning of the membrane influences its lifetime. Keywords: membranes, nanofiltration, heavy metal, removal, wastewater 1. Introduction Surface and groundwater resources are at risk of degradation and pollution due to heavy metal ions present in discharges from various industries. The harmful effects of heavy metal ions on human health require their complete removal from various wastewaters using advanced treatment technologies [1]. The manufacturing processes of various goods, such as paints, vehicle batteries, pigments, and fertilizers, mainly lead to the pollution of water supplies [2]. Overexposure to heavy metal ions can cause severe diseases to humans and animals [3]. Table 1 shows some of the heavy metals present in wastewater, their effects on human health [4], and their concentrations permitted in wastewater according to NTPA 001/2002 [5]. Conventional methods for wastewater treatment polluted with heavy metal ions include electrochemical treatment, flotation, ion exchange, and chemical precipitation [6,7,8]. Each method has its own restrictions, such as the formation of a huge amount of sludge in the chemical precipitation approach [9,10], low treatment efficiency, high resin cost, and problems in regenerating spent resin in the ion exchange process [11,12]. The most commonly used membrane materials are polymeric, ceramic, and hybrid substances [14], but the use of polymeric membranes is the preferred choice due to their ease of operation, excellent selectivity rates, and surface modification [15]. Microfiltration (MF), nanofiltration (NF), ultrafiltration (UF), and reverse osmosis (RO) are the four classifications of membranes used for membrane-based technologies [16]. However, RO and NF have become the most suitable technologies for water treatment and desalination [17,18,19]. Nanofiltration (NF) is a membrane-based separation technique that utilizes hydrostatic pressure to transport molecules across semipermeable membranes (Figure 1). This method allows low-molecular-weight solutes and solvents to move through the membrane while larger molecules are trapped. NF membranes have a molecular weight threshold of around 400–500 Da, have pore diameters between 0.5 and 2 nm, and require working pressures in the range of 10–50 bar. They have the capacity of retaining neutral species with a molecular weight between 200 and 300 g/mol and reject inorganic ions through a combination of electrostatic interactions between the charged membrane and the ions and size exclusion [20,21]. NF provides several advantages over other membrane technologies, such as stronger rejection of higher flux and divalent ions, reduced energy usage, and lower operating pressure. This makes it a promising technology for removing oil and grease, suspended particles, heavy metals, dyes, and other chemicals from industrial effluents and drinking water [22,23]. fetched_contents.text: Comparison of Nanofiltration with Reverse Osmosis in Reclaiming Tertiary Treated Municipal Wastewater for Irrigation Purposes Abstract This study compares the performance of nanofiltration (NF) and reverse osmosis (RO) for the reclamation of ultrafiltered municipal wastewater for irrigation of food crops. RO and NF technologies were evaluated at different applied pressures; the performance of each technology was evaluated in terms of water flux, recovery rate, specific energy consumption and quality of permeate. It was found that the permeate from the reverse osmosis (RO) process complied with Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) standards at pressures applied between 10 and 18 bar. At an applied pressure of 20 bar, the permeate quality did not comply with irrigation water standards in terms of chloride, sodium and calcium concentration. It was found that nanofiltration process was not suitable for the reclamation of wastewater as the concentration of chloride, sodium and calcium exceeded the allowable limits at all applied pressures. In the reverse osmosis process, the highest recovery rate was 36%, which was achieved at a pressure of 16 bar. The specific energy consumption at this applied pressure was 0.56 kWh/m3. The lowest specific energy of 0.46 kWh/m3 was achieved at an applied pressure of 12 bar with a water recovery rate of 32.7%. Keywords: irrigation water, reverse osmosis, nanofiltration, treated sewage effluent, water reuse 1. Introduction Water scarcity is a major challenge that affects food security worldwide, particularly in arid regions. The United Nations (UN) estimates that agriculture accounts for 70% of water usage around the world [1]. Municipal treated wastewater could be an economical solution to be used as irrigation water and a source of nutrients [2]. Nanofiltration improves wastewater treatment efficiency by selectively removing a broad range of contaminants, while maintaining lower energy and cost burdens than some alternatives. The core separation mechanism combines steric hindrance, electric exclusion, dielectric effect, and hydration, with rejection also depending on membrane charge and pore size [N1-F1]. NF membranes have a pore size of 1 nm and a molecular weight cutoff (MWCO) of 300 to 500 Da, and their surface charge depends on functional groups, which explains why charged contaminants are more strongly rejected [N1-R1][N1-F1]. This makes NF especially effective for polyvalent anions, cations, uncharged compounds, suspended particles, heavy metals, salts, organics, and dyes [N1-F1][N2-F2]. 

For industrial wastewater, NF is particularly useful for removing heavy metals, salts, and organic pollutants. The review evidence shows that NF membranes are increasingly used for heavy metal removal because they can be tailored by modification methods such as interfacial polymerization, grafting, and nano-filler addition, with reported high efficiencies such as 99.90% for Cr³⁺ removal and strong rejection of salts like K₂SO₄, MgSO₄, KCl, and NaCl [N2-F2][N2-R4]. The industrial wastewater case studies cited in the search evidence also show NF being applied to streams such as color rinse, alkaline pickling rinse, acidic baths, and other industrial rinse waters [N2-R3][N2-R5]. This is important because many industrial effluents contain multiple contaminant classes, and NF’s intermediate molecular weight cutoff allows it to reject both small ions/salts and larger organic/metallic species without requiring the high pressure of reverse osmosis [N1-F1][N2-F2].

In terms of membrane pore size and charge, smaller pores and a charged surface enhance rejection by steric and electrostatic mechanisms, but pore size also affects flux: narrower pores increase selectivity while potentially lowering hydraulic conductivity [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. The review evidence also notes that pore aspect ratio and pore size distribution are important, with higher aspect ratio improving performance and wider distribution worsening it [N1-F1]. This explains why NF is often optimized for a balance between rejection and flux rather than operating at maximum rejection alone.

Compared to other membrane processes, nanofiltration is more energy-efficient than reverse osmosis because it operates at lower pressures and consumes less energy per cubic meter of treated water [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The comparison study found that RO required high applied pressure (minimum 40 bar) and produced permeate that could exceed irrigation standards for chloride, sodium, and calcium, whereas NF was not suitable for wastewater reclamation in that study because its permeate quality still exceeded allowable limits at all pressures [N3-F3]. At the same time, NF is less energy-intensive than RO, but not as low-pressure as ultrafiltration; the evidence emphasizes that RO and NF are among the most suitable technologies for water treatment and desalination, with NF offering reduced energy use and lower operating pressure [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Cost effectiveness is also a key advantage: NF membranes are described as cost-effective and have lower capital and normalized cost burdens relative to electrodialysis, with industry estimates showing ED at over 200 $ m⁻² versus RO below 10 $ m⁻² [N1-F1][N3-F3]. 

Overall, nanofiltration improves wastewater treatment efficiency by combining strong contaminant rejection with relatively low energy and cost, especially for multicontaminant industrial streams. Its effectiveness is rooted in its intermediate MWCO, surface charge, and pressure-driven operation, which allow it to remove heavy metals, salts, organics, and other pollutants while staying more economical and energy-efficient than RO in many cases [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

The evidence also notes that hybrid membranes, such as thin film composite (TFC) membranes, are commercially used for heavy metal removal, high water permeability, and strong mechanical and chemical stability [N2-F2]. These modifications help NF membranes better reject contaminants and resist fouling, which is a major benefit in industrial settings.

The evidence also shows that these innovations can improve industrial wastewater treatment outcomes. The review of advanced NF membranes for heavy-metal removal reports very high treatment efficiencies, including 99.90% Cr³⁺ removal using PVAM and GA membranes [N2-F2]. The hybrid NF-RO process in the tertiary wastewater study was capable of producing permeate that met irrigation water standards, showing that hybridization can overcome NF’s limitations in certain applications [N3-F3]. The industrial wastewater case studies also support real-world relevance: NF has been used to treat color rinse, alkaline pickling rinse, acidic baths, and secondary effluents from textile mills or other industrial treatment plants [N2-R3][N2-R5][N6-R5]. Although the excerpts do not provide detailed case metrics, they establish that NF is being deployed in practical industrial streams and that pretreatment/hybrid approaches are actively used to improve performance [N5-R2][N5-R1].

## 6) Industrial implementation evidence and real-world efficiency gains

Industrial implementation evidence shows that nanofiltration is applied to a variety of actual industrial wastewater streams. The evidence specifically mentions color rinse, alkaline pickling rinse, acidic baths, and secondary effluents from textile mills or other industrial treatment plants [N2-R3][N2-R5][N6-R5]. The anodizing industry case study used NF to treat wastewater from individual baths such as color rinse, alkaline pickling rinse, and acidic baths, illustrating that NF is used in process-specific industrial settings rather than only in general municipal reuse [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3]. The case study on Eternal Electronic (Suzhou, China) Co., Ltd. also analyzed different membrane materials for treating wastewater discharged by that company, showing that NF is being evaluated in real industrial operations for recovery and reuse [N6-R4]. This indicates that NF is not just a laboratory concept but a deployed treatment technology in industrial wastewater management.

Reported recovery, reuse, or resource recovery benefits are evident in the evidence. The tertiary wastewater study showed that a hybrid NF-RO process could produce permeate meeting irrigation water standards, implying recovery and reuse of treated water for agricultural or industrial purposes [N3-F3]. The anodizing case study likewise suggests that NF is used to treat and possibly recover rinse waters, which can be valuable for industrial water conservation and closed-loop reuse [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3]. The heavy-metal removal review also emphasizes that NF membranes are attractive for wastewater treatment because they can be tailored to remove pollutants and are adaptable to different circumstances, which supports resource recovery by enabling selective removal of contaminants rather than simply discharging effluent [N2-F2]. In addition, the evidence indicates that pretreatment and hybrid systems can improve nutrient and contaminant removal, which is relevant for resource recovery by preserving valuable nutrients or reducing downstream treatment needs [N5-R2][N3-F3].

However, the evidence also highlights limitations and conditions under which performance is optimal. The tertiary wastewater study found that NF was not suitable for wastewater reclamation in that particular application because permeate quality still exceeded allowable limits at all pressures, suggesting that NF’s effectiveness depends on feed composition, contaminant load, and operating conditions [N3-F3]. The fouling and cleaning study notes that membrane pollution reduces water yield and increases operation and maintenance costs, and that repeated cleaning influences membrane lifetime [N4-R1]. This means that performance is optimal when fouling is minimized, operating pressure and flux are balanced, and pretreatment is used to reduce fouling precursors [N4-R1][N4-R4][N5-R2]. The comparison study also shows that NF requires careful pressure control, since higher pressure can improve rejection but may not always yield acceptable water quality [N3-F3]. Overall, industrial implementation evidence demonstrates that nanofiltration can achieve recovery and reuse benefits, especially when combined with pretreatment or hybrid systems, but its performance is highly dependent on the specific wastewater stream and operating conditions [N2-R3][N6-R1][N3-F3].

---

## Conclusion

Nanofiltration membranes enhance industrial wastewater treatment efficiency by selectively rejecting a broad range of contaminants, including heavy metals, salts, organics, and suspended solids, while operating at lower pressures and lower energy costs than reverse osmosis [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]. Their separation efficiency depends on pore size, charge, and MWCO, with narrower pores and charged surfaces improving rejection but requiring careful optimization of flux and pressure [N1-R1][N1-F1][N1-R2]. At the same time, NF faces operational challenges such as fouling, scaling, and the need for cleaning and regeneration, which increase maintenance costs and shorten membrane life [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4]. Recent innovations, including hybrid systems, advanced oxidation, and material modifications, help overcome these limitations and improve contaminant removal and fouling resistance [N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-F2]. Industrial implementation evidence shows that NF is already being used in real-world settings to treat color rinse, alkaline pickling rinse, acidic baths, and secondary effluents, with reported benefits for recovery, reuse, and resource recovery [N2-R3][N2-R5][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3]. In practice, NF’s efficiency gains are strongest when it is integrated with pretreatment or hybrid systems and operated under conditions that balance rejection, flux, and fouling control [N3-F3][N5-R2][N4-R1].

Nanofiltration improves wastewater treatment efficiency by selectively removing a broad range of contaminants, while maintaining lower energy and cost burdens than some alternatives. The core separation mechanism combines steric hindrance, electric exclusion, dielectric effect, and hydration, with rejection also depending on membrane charge and pore size [N1-F1]. NF membranes have a pore size of 1 nm and a molecular weight cutoff (MWCO) of 300 to 500 Da, and their surface charge depends on functional groups, which explains why charged contaminants are more strongly rejected [N1-R1][N1-F1]. This makes NF especially effective for polyvalent anions, cations, uncharged compounds, suspended particles, heavy metals, salts, organics, and dyes [N1-F1][N2-F2]. 

For industrial wastewater, NF is particularly useful for removing heavy metals, salts, and organic pollutants. The review evidence shows that NF membranes are increasingly used for heavy metal removal because they can be tailored by modification methods such as interfacial polymerization, grafting, and nano-filler addition, with reported high efficiencies such as 99.90% for Cr³⁺ removal and strong rejection of salts like K₂SO₄, MgSO₄, KCl, and NaCl [N2-F2][N2-R4]. The industrial wastewater case studies cited in the search evidence also show NF being applied to streams such as color rinse, alkaline pickling rinse, acidic baths, and other industrial rinse waters [N2-R3][N2-R5]. This is important because many industrial effluents contain multiple contaminant classes, and NF’s intermediate molecular weight cutoff allows it to reject both small ions/salts and larger organic/metallic species without requiring the high pressure of reverse osmosis [N1-F1][N2-F2].

In terms of membrane pore size and charge, smaller pores and a charged surface enhance rejection by steric and electrostatic mechanisms, but pore size also affects flux: narrower pores increase selectivity while potentially lowering hydraulic conductivity [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. The review evidence also notes that pore aspect ratio and pore size distribution are important, with higher aspect ratio improving performance and wider distribution worsening it [N1-F1]. This explains why NF is often optimized for a balance between rejection and flux rather than operating at maximum rejection alone.

Compared to other membrane processes, nanofiltration is more energy-efficient than reverse osmosis because it operates at lower pressures and consumes less energy per cubic meter of treated water [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5]. The comparison study found that RO required high applied pressure (minimum 40 bar) and produced permeate that could exceed irrigation standards for chloride, sodium, and calcium, whereas NF was not suitable for wastewater reclamation in that study because its permeate quality still exceeded allowable limits at all pressures [N3-F3]. At the same time, NF is less energy-intensive than RO, but not as low-pressure as ultrafiltration; the evidence emphasizes that RO and NF are among the most suitable technologies for water treatment and desalination, with NF offering reduced energy use and lower operating pressure [N1-F1][N3-F3]. Cost effectiveness is also a key advantage: NF membranes are described as cost-effective and have lower capital and normalized cost burdens relative to electrodialysis, with industry estimates showing ED at over 200 $ m⁻² versus RO below 10 $ m⁻² [N1-F1][N3-F3]. 

Overall, nanofiltration improves wastewater treatment efficiency by combining strong contaminant rejection with relatively low energy and cost, especially for multicontaminant industrial streams. Its effectiveness is rooted in its intermediate MWCO, surface charge, and pressure-driven operation, which allow it to remove heavy metals, salts, organics, and other pollutants while staying more economical and energy-efficient than RO in many cases [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3].

Nanofiltration faces major practical challenges in industrial wastewater treatment, particularly fouling and scaling. The search evidence directly states that membrane pollution reduces water yield and increases operation and maintenance costs, making fouling control an urgent problem [N4-R1]. It also identifies fouling as a key challenge in municipal wastewater treatment, with variation depending on operational conditions [N4-R5]. The broader challenges and solutions review explicitly notes the trade-off between selectivity and flux, where high rejection rates often come with low flux, and membrane fouling is a major issue, including adsorption-related fouling [N4-R2]. This means that in industrial settings, NF membranes are vulnerable to both particulate and organic fouling, which can degrade flux and increase cleaning demands.

Cleaning, regeneration, and maintenance requirements are therefore substantial. The fouling and cleaning study emphasizes that correctly identifying foulants is essential for determining corrective measures and proper cleaning protocols [N4-R4]. The review also states that repeated cleaning influences membrane lifetime, which implies that cleaning is not merely a periodic maintenance task but a recurring operational burden that shortens membrane service life [N2-F2][N4-R1]. In industrial wastewater, where organic, inorganic, and particulate contaminants coexist, this means that cleaning schedules, chemical regimens, and frequency must be tightly managed to maintain performance while preserving membrane integrity.

Operational limits such as pressure, temperature, and flux are central to NF’s performance. The comparison study notes that NF membranes operate in the pressure range of 10–50 bar and that permeate quality in wastewater treatment depends on applied pressure [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The NF vs RO comparison found that RO required high pressure (minimum 40 bar) and produced permeate that exceeded irrigation standards at higher pressures, whereas NF was not suitable for wastewater reclamation in that study because its permeate still exceeded allowable limits at all pressures [N3-F3]. This shows that pressure is not only an operational constraint but also a performance determinant: higher pressure can improve rejection but may also worsen fouling or scaling, and may not always yield acceptable water quality. The evidence also points to feed concentration, feed flow rate, feed temperature, permeate vapor pressure, and applied pressure as factors affecting membrane performance [N1-F1]. Temperature and flux are similarly important because membrane performance is sensitive to operating conditions, and the review explicitly notes that pore aspect ratio and pore size distribution affect performance [N1-F1]. 

Taken together, the practical challenges of NF in industrial wastewater treatment are significant: fouling and scaling reduce yield and increase costs, cleaning and regeneration are necessary but shorten membrane life, and pressure, temperature, and flux must be carefully balanced to avoid operational inefficiencies [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4][N1-F1][N3-F3]. These trade-offs make NF highly efficient in theory but operationally demanding in practice, especially in industrial settings where contaminant load and variability are high.

## How nanofiltration membranes enhance industrial wastewater treatment efficiency

Nanofiltration membranes improve industrial wastewater treatment efficiency by combining strong contaminant rejection with relatively low energy and cost burdens, making them a practical choice for complex effluent streams. At the same time, they face operational challenges such as fouling, scaling, and trade-offs between rejection and flux. Recent innovations, including hybrid systems and advanced materials, further extend their performance, while industrial implementation evidence shows that NF is already being used in real-world settings to recover and reuse water. Below is a structured synthesis of how nanofiltration membranes enhance wastewater treatment efficiency.

---

## 1) Why nanofiltration is effective for industrial wastewater

Nanofiltration membranes are particularly effective because they selectively remove a broad range of contaminants. The core separation mechanism combines steric hindrance, electric exclusion, dielectric effect, and hydration, with rejection also depending on membrane charge and pore size [N1-F1]. NF membranes typically have a pore size of 1 nm and a molecular weight cutoff (MWCO) of 300 to 500 Da, and their surface charge depends on functional groups, which explains why charged contaminants are more strongly rejected [N1-R1][N1-F1]. This makes NF especially useful for removing polyvalent anions, cations, uncharged compounds, suspended particles, heavy metals, salts, organics, and dyes [N1-F1][N2-F2].

For industrial wastewater, NF is especially valuable because many effluent streams contain multiple contaminant classes. The evidence shows that NF is increasingly used for heavy metal removal because membranes can be tailored by modification methods such as interfacial polymerization, grafting, and nano-filler addition [N2-F2]. It also reports high removal efficiencies for salts like K₂SO₄, MgSO₄, KCl, and NaCl, as well as heavy metals such as As³⁺ and Cr³⁺ [N2-R4][N2-F2]. Industrial wastewater case studies show NF being applied to streams such as color rinse, alkaline pickling rinse, acidic baths, and secondary effluents from textile mills or other industrial treatment plants [N2-R3][N2-R5][N6-R5]. This is important because industrial wastewater often contains a mixture of inorganic salts, organics, and metals, and NF’s intermediate MWCO allows it to reject small ions and larger organic/metallic species without requiring the high pressure of reverse osmosis [N1-F1][N2-F2].

---

## 2) How pore size and charge affect separation efficiency

The membrane’s pore size and charge are central to its separation efficiency. A narrower pore size increases selectivity by enhancing steric hindrance, while a charged surface improves rejection through electric exclusion and other electrostatic interactions [N1-F1][N1-R1]. The review evidence also notes that pore aspect ratio and pore size distribution are important: higher aspect ratio improves performance, while wider distribution worsens it [N1-F1]. This explains why NF is often optimized for a balance between rejection and flux rather than operating at maximum rejection alone.

The MWCO is another key factor. NF membranes have MWCO in the range of 300–500 Da, and the review explicitly states that this range is important for determining which contaminants can be rejected [N1-R2][N1-R3]. This means that NF is well suited to removing ions, small organic molecules, and some larger molecules, but not as effective as reverse osmosis for very small molecules or salts when operating pressure is not carefully managed [N1-F1][N2-F2]. Overall, the combination of pore size, charge, and MWCO makes NF a versatile membrane for industrial wastewater treatment.

## 3) How nanofiltration compares to other membrane processes in energy and cost

Nanofiltration is more energy-efficient than reverse osmosis because it operates at lower pressures and consumes less energy per cubic meter of treated water [N3-F3][N3-R2][N3-R5]. This shows that NF can achieve high-quality water with less pressure, which is a major operational and energy advantage.

Cost effectiveness is also a key benefit. In comparison with other membrane processes, NF is less energy-intensive than RO and more selective than ultrafiltration, making it an attractive choice for wastewater treatment where energy and cost are important constraints [N1-F1][N3-F3].
